subtopics.title: Object-Oriented Fundamentals, Models & Development Cycle
subtopics.subtitle: Objects, classes, the four pillars, OMT's three models and the Unified Process phases

concepts.text: Objects and Classes

Object-oriented (OO) development models a system as a collection of cooperating objects rather than as a hierarchy of functions. An object is a concrete entity with state (the current values of its attributes), behaviour (the operations it can perform) and identity (what distinguishes it from every other object, even one with identical state). A class is the template or blueprint that describes the attributes and operations shared by a set of objects; each object is an instance of exactly one class. Objects collaborate by message passing: one object asks another to execute one of its operations, possibly passing arguments and receiving a result.
The Four Pillars (APIE)
The four pillars of OOP, remembered as APIE:
items: Abstraction: hiding complexity by exposing only the essential features of an entity relevant to the problem, e.g. a Car class exposing start() and brake() but not fuel-injection timing.

Polymorphism: one interface, many forms. Compile-time (static) polymorphism is method overloading (same name, different parameter lists, resolved by the compiler); run-time (dynamic) polymorphism is method overriding (subclass redefines an inherited method, resolved by dynamic binding through a base-class reference).
Inheritance: a child (sub) class reuses and extends the attributes and operations of a parent (super) class, forming an is-a hierarchy; it supports reuse and generalisation-specialisation.
Encapsulation: bundling data and the methods that operate on it into one unit while restricting direct access to the data (private fields, public methods); it realises Parnas' information hiding.

concepts.text: Other core OO concepts that MCQs test:
items: Message passing: the only way objects interact; a message names the receiver, the operation and the arguments.
Abstract class: cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract (unimplemented) operations; an interface declares operations only and is realised by classes.
Multiple inheritance: a class with more than one parent (allowed in C++, avoided in Java which uses multiple interfaces instead); can cause the diamond problem.

Relationships between classes: association (general link), aggregation (weak has-a, hollow diamond, parts exist independently), composition (strong has-a, filled diamond, parts destroyed with the whole), generalisation (is-a).

concepts.text: Defining Models: Rumbaugh's OMT

A model is an abstraction of a system built to understand it before building it; it omits non-essential detail. Rumbaugh's Object Modeling Technique (OMT), one of the three methods merged into UML, describes a system with three complementary models. Each model captures one view, and together they describe what the system is, when things happen and how values are computed.

rows: Static structure: objects, classes, attributes, operations, relationships
Temporal and control aspects: events, states, sequences of operations
Data value transformations: what is computed from what

concepts.text: Object-Oriented Development Cycle and the Unified Process

The OO development cycle proceeds from object-oriented analysis (OOA: find and describe the concepts in the problem domain), through object-oriented design (OOD: define software objects and how they collaborate), to object-oriented programming (OOP: implement the design classes in an OO language), followed by testing. The Unified Process (UP, commercially RUP) organises this work as an iterative, incremental, use-case-driven, architecture-centric and risk-focused process. Each iteration is a short time-boxed mini-project (typically 2–6 weeks) that produces a tested, integrated, executable partial system.

rows: Vision, business case, scope, rough estimates; go/no-go decision
Refine vision, build and stabilise core architecture, resolve high risks, find most requirements
Iteratively implement remaining lower-risk, easier elements; prepare for deployment
Beta tests, deployment to users, training, fixes

concepts.text: UP disciplines (workflows) run across all phases with varying intensity:
items: Business modeling (domain model), Requirements (use-case model, supplementary specification), Analysis and design (design model), Implementation, Test and Deployment.
Supporting disciplines: configuration and change management, project management and environment.
Inception is not the requirements phase: in the UP most requirements are discovered during elaboration iterations.
Superimposing waterfall on UP (all requirements first, then all design) is a classic misunderstanding that MCQs often probe.

concepts.latex: WMC = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i,\qquad DIT(C) = \text{depth of } C \text{ from root}
concepts.plainText: WMC = sum of complexities c_i of the n methods of a class; DIT(C) = depth of class C in the inheritance tree (root = 0)

formulas.plainText: WMC (weighted methods per class) = c_1 + c_2 + ... + c_n

formulas.latex: DIT(C) = \text{edges from root to } C,\quad NOC(C) = \text{immediate subclasses}
formulas.plainText: DIT(C) = number of edges from the root to C; NOC(C) = number of immediate subclasses of C

notes.text: Overloading = compile-time = static binding; overriding = run-time = dynamic binding and needs inheritance. Encapsulation is about bundling and access control; abstraction is about showing only essential features.
UP phase order is Inception, Elaboration, Construction, Transition (I-E-C-T). The architecture is baselined at the end of Elaboration, and each phase contains one or more iterations.
Do not confuse OMT's functional model (DFDs, value computations) with the dynamic model (state diagrams, control over time). The object model is the static one.

formulas.title: Anatomy of an object
formulas.description: Every object has attribute values (state), operations (behaviour) and a unique identity independent of its state.

formulas.title: Weighted methods per class (CK)
formulas.description: Sum of the complexities of a class's methods; with unit complexity it equals the method count, and high values suggest a class that is hard to reuse.

formulas.title: Depth of inheritance tree and number of children
formulas.latex: DIT(C) = \text{edges from root to } C,\quad NOC(C) = \text{immediate subclasses}
formulas.plainText: DIT(C) = edges from root to C; NOC(C) = number of immediate subclasses
formulas.description: Deeper DIT means more inherited behaviour and higher complexity; larger NOC means more reuse but more classes affected by a change.

flashcards.front: Name the four pillars of OOP (APIE).
What are the three models of Rumbaugh's OMT?
flashcards.back: Object model (static structure, class diagrams), dynamic model (states and events, state diagrams) and functional model (value transformations, DFDs).

flashcards.front: List the four Unified Process phases in order.
flashcards.back: Inception, Elaboration, Construction, Transition; the architecture is stabilised during Elaboration.

flashcards.front: How does run-time polymorphism differ from compile-time polymorphism?
flashcards.back: Run-time polymorphism uses overriding and dynamic binding on the object's actual type; compile-time polymorphism uses overloading resolved by the compiler from argument types.

questions.questionText: Declaring a class's fields private and allowing access only through public methods primarily implements which OO principle?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation bundles data with its methods and restricts direct access to the data, realising information hiding.

questions.questionText: In the Unified Process, the phase whose main goal is to build and stabilise the core architecture and resolve the high-risk elements is:
questions.explanation: Elaboration iterations implement the risky core architecture and discover most requirements, ending with the Lifecycle Architecture milestone.

questions.questionText: In Rumbaugh's OMT, which model describes the temporal and control aspects of a system using state diagrams?
questions.explanation: The dynamic model captures events, states and sequencing over time using state diagrams; the functional model uses DFDs and the object model uses class diagrams.

questions.questionText: Class D extends C, C extends B and B extends A, where A is the root of the hierarchy (DIT = 0). What is the depth of inheritance tree (DIT) of class D?
questions.explanation: DIT counts edges from the root: A to B is 1, B to C is 2 and C to D is 3.

subtopics.title: The Requirement Process & Use Cases
subtopics.subtitle: FURPS+, actors, use case formats and scenarios, include/extend and use case diagrams

concepts.text: The Requirement Process

Requirements are the capabilities and conditions to which the system, and more broadly the project, must conform. In an iterative OO process such as the UP, requirements are not frozen up front: they are discovered and refined across iterations through elicitation, analysis, specification, validation and management of change. The main UP requirements artefacts are the use-case model (functional requirements as stories), the supplementary specification (non-functional requirements), the glossary (terms and data definitions), the vision (high-level goals) and business rules.
FURPS+ categorises the requirements to be captured:
items: Functional: features, capabilities, security.
Usability: human factors, help, documentation.
Reliability: frequency of failure, recoverability, predictability.
Performance: response times, throughput, accuracy, availability, resource usage.
Supportability: adaptability, maintainability, internationalisation, configurability.
The '+' covers implementation constraints, interface, operations, packaging and legal requirements.

concepts.text: Use Cases and Actors

A use case is a collection of related success and failure scenarios that describe an actor using the system to achieve a goal; a scenario (use case instance) is one specific sequence of actions and interactions. Use cases are text documents first; the use case diagram is only a context summary. The basic components of use case modelling are the actor, the use case and the system boundary. Good use cases pass the boss test, the elementary business process (EBP) test (one person, one place, one time, measurable business value) and the size test (usually several steps, not a single step).

rows: Has user goals fulfilled by using the system
Provides a service to the system
Has an interest in the behaviour but does not interact directly

concepts.text: Use Case Formats and Sections

rows: Terse one-paragraph summary, usually the main success scenario
All steps and variations with supporting sections
Important, high-risk use cases in elaboration

concepts.text: Sections of a fully dressed use case (Cockburn/Larman template):
items: Use case name (starts with a verb, e.g. Process Sale), scope (system under design), level (user-goal or subfunction), primary actor.
Stakeholders and interests: whose interests the behaviour must satisfy.
Preconditions: what must be true on start and is not tested in the use case; success guarantee (postconditions): what must be true on successful completion.
Main success scenario (basic flow, happy path): the typical unconditional path to the goal, written as numbered steps.
Extensions (alternate flows): all other success and failure branches, labelled against the step they branch from, e.g. 3a, *a.
Special requirements, technology and data variations, frequency of occurrence and open issues.

concepts.text:
Use Case UC1: Process Sale   Primary actor: Cashier
Main success scenario:
 1. Customer arrives at POS checkout with goods.
 2. Cashier starts a new sale.
 3. Cashier enters item identifier.
 4. System records sale line item and presents description, price, running total.
    Cashier repeats steps 3-4 until done.
 5. System presents total with taxes calculated.
 6. Customer pays and System handles payment.
Extensions:
 3a. Invalid identifier: System signals error and rejects entry.
Use Case Relationships and Diagrams

rows: Base use case always (mandatorily) uses shared behaviour of another
Dashed arrow from base to included use case
Extension adds optional behaviour at an extension point of the base, under a condition
Dashed arrow from extending use case to base
Child use case or actor specialises a parent
Solid line with hollow triangle towards parent
Actor participates in (communicates with) a use case
Solid line between actor and use case

concepts.text: A use case diagram shows the system boundary as a rectangle, use cases as ovals inside it and actors (stick figures, or boxes stereotyped «actor» for systems) outside it. Primary actors are conventionally placed on the left and supporting actors on the right. The diagram is a context overview; the real value of use case modelling lies in the written scenarios, which drive design, testing and the user manual.
Estimating from Use Cases: Use Case Points

concepts.plainText: UCP = (UUCW + UAW) x TCF x ECF

concepts.text: Karner's use case points weights:
items: Use case weight (UUCW): simple (≤ 3 transactions) = 5, average (4–7) = 10, complex (> 7) = 15.
Actor weight (UAW): simple (another system via API) = 1, average (system via protocol or text interface) = 2, complex (human via GUI) = 3.
Technical complexity factor TCF = 0.6 + 0.01 × TFactor (13 weighted technical factors).
Environmental factor ECF = 1.4 − 0.03 × EFactor (8 weighted team and environment factors).

formulas.plainText: UCP = (UUCW + UAW) x TCF x ECF

notes.text: «include» = mandatory, arrow from base to included; «extend» = optional and conditional, arrow from the extending use case back to the base. The arrow direction is a common MCQ trap.
Use cases are primarily text. A use case diagram without written scenarios captures almost none of the functional requirements.
Preconditions are assumed true and not checked within the use case; the success guarantee is what must hold after success. Do not swap them.

formulas.title: Use case points
formulas.plainText: UCP = (UUCW + UAW) x TCF x ECF
formulas.description: Karner's size estimate: unadjusted use case and actor weights scaled by technical and environmental factors.

formulas.title: Unadjusted use case weight
formulas.plainText: UUCW = 5 x simple + 10 x average + 15 x complex use cases
formulas.description: Use cases are weighted by transaction count: up to 3 simple, 4 to 7 average, more than 7 complex.

formulas.title: Technical complexity factor
formulas.description: Adjusts size for 13 weighted technical factors such as distribution, performance and reusability.

formulas.title: Environmental complexity factor
formulas.description: Adjusts size for 8 team and environment factors; a more experienced team gives a smaller ECF.

flashcards.front: Distinguish primary, supporting and offstage actors.
flashcards.back: Primary actors have goals fulfilled by the system, supporting actors provide services to it, and offstage actors have an interest in its behaviour without interacting directly.

flashcards.front: What are the three use case formats?
flashcards.back: Brief (one-paragraph main success scenario), casual (informal paragraphs for several scenarios) and fully dressed (all steps, variations and supporting sections).

flashcards.front: What is the main success scenario and what are extensions?
flashcards.back: The main success scenario is the typical happy path to the goal; extensions are all the alternative success and failure branches from its steps.
Functional, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability, plus constraints such as implementation, interface, operations, packaging and legal.

questions.questionText: In a use case diagram, 'Print Gift Receipt' adds optional behaviour at an extension point of 'Process Sale' only when the customer asks for it. How is this modelled?
options: «extend», dashed arrow from Print Gift Receipt to Process Sale
«include», dashed arrow from Process Sale to Print Gift Receipt
«extend», dashed arrow from Process Sale to Print Gift Receipt
Generalisation, solid line with hollow triangle towards Process Sale
questions.explanation: Optional, conditional behaviour is an «extend» relationship, and the dashed arrow points from the extending use case to the base use case.

questions.questionText: In a POS system, an external credit-card authorisation service that the system calls during Process Sale is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: A supporting actor provides a service to the system under discussion; the cashier is the primary actor and the tax agency is an offstage actor.

questions.questionText: A project has 4 simple, 3 average and 2 complex use cases, and 2 simple, 1 average and 2 complex actors. With TCF = 1.0 and ECF = 0.9, the use case points (UCP) are:
Which use case format includes stakeholders and interests, preconditions, a success guarantee, the main success scenario and all extensions?
questions.explanation: The fully dressed format documents all steps and variations with supporting sections; brief and casual formats are short, informal summaries.

subtopics.title: UML & Building the Conceptual (Domain) Model
subtopics.subtitle: UML diagram families, domain models, finding conceptual classes and description classes

concepts.text: The Unified Modeling Language

The Unified Modeling Language (UML) is a standard visual language for specifying, constructing, visualising and documenting the artefacts of software systems. It was created by the Three Amigos, Grady Booch (Booch method), James Rumbaugh (OMT) and Ivar Jacobson (OOSE and use cases), and was adopted as a standard by the Object Management Group (OMG) in 1997. UML is a notation, not a process: it can be used with the UP, agile methods or any other process. It can be applied as a sketch, as a blueprint or as a programming language (model-driven development).

rows: Class, Object, Component, Deployment, Package, Composite structure, Profile
What the system is made of

concepts.text: What each commonly tested diagram shows:
items: Class diagram: classes, attributes, operations and relationships; object diagram: a snapshot of instances and links at one moment.
Component diagram: modular replaceable parts and their interfaces; deployment diagram: physical nodes and the artefacts deployed on them; package diagram: grouping and dependencies.
Sequence diagram: interactions ordered in time along lifelines; communication (collaboration) diagram: the same messages numbered on a network of linked objects, emphasising relationships.
State machine diagram: states and event-triggered transitions of one object; activity diagram: flowchart-like workflow with actions, decisions, forks, joins and swimlanes.
Timing diagram: state changes against a time axis; interaction overview: an activity diagram whose nodes are interactions.

concepts.text: The Domain (Conceptual) Model

A domain model is a visual representation of conceptual classes or real-situation objects in a domain, drawn as a UML class diagram with no operations. It shows conceptual classes, associations between them and their attributes. It is the most important artefact of OO analysis: it builds a shared vocabulary and inspires the names of software classes in the design model, lowering the representational gap between how we think of the domain and how the code is structured. It is built iteratively, usually for the use cases chosen in the current iteration.
A domain model does NOT show:
items: Software artefacts such as windows, databases, controllers or DAO classes (unless the domain itself is software).
Responsibilities or methods: operations belong to design class diagrams.
Foreign-key style attributes: relationships are shown as associations, not as ID fields.

concepts.text: A conceptual class is an idea, thing or object in the domain. Larman describes it by its symbol (the words or image representing it), its intension (its definition) and its extension (the set of examples to which it applies). For example, Sale has the symbol 'Sale', the intension 'a purchase transaction event with a date and time' and an extension of all the sales that occur.
Identifying Conceptual Classes
Three strategies for finding conceptual classes:
items: Reuse or modify existing models: published domain and analysis patterns for common domains such as inventory, finance or health.

Use a category list: business transactions (Sale, Payment), transaction line items (SalesLineItem), products or services (Item), where transactions are recorded (Register, Ledger), roles of people (Cashier, Customer), places (Store), events, physical objects, descriptions of things (ProductDescription), catalogues, containers, other collaborating systems, records of finance and contracts.

Noun phrase identification (linguistic analysis): underline nouns and noun phrases in fully dressed use cases as candidates, then filter them, because natural language is ambiguous and some nouns are attributes or synonyms.

rows: Thought of as a number (Money data type)
Report of information already in Sale; include only if it has its own rules, e.g. returns
Synonyms: keep a single name in the glossary

concepts.text: Description Classes and Domain vs Design Model

A description class contains information that describes something else, such as ProductDescription (price, description, itemID) describing many physical Item instances. It is needed when deleting instances of the described things would lose information (if all items are sold, the price is still known), when there are groups of items or services that share the same description, and to reduce redundant or duplicated information. FlightDescription describing many Flight occurrences is another classic example.

rows: Visibility markers, typed attributes and navigability

formulas.plainText: A_max = n(n - 1)/2 possible binary associations among n conceptual classes

notes.text: Structural diagrams answer 'what is it made of' (class, object, component, deployment, package, composite structure, profile); everything else, including use case, is behavioural. Sequence, communication, timing and interaction overview are the interaction diagrams.
A domain model is not a picture of software objects and not a data model: no methods, no UI or database classes, and no foreign-key attributes.
When in doubt whether to include a candidate conceptual class, include it: in domain modelling it is better to over-specify with many fine-grained classes than to under-specify.

formulas.title: UML 2.5 diagram count
formulas.description: UML 2.5 defines seven structural and seven behavioural diagram types, four of the behavioural ones being interaction diagrams.

formulas.title: Parts of a conceptual class
formulas.description: A conceptual class has a name or image, a definition, and the set of real instances it applies to.

formulas.title: Possible binary associations
formulas.description: The number of distinct class pairs that could be linked among n conceptual classes, which is why only need-to-know associations are drawn.

flashcards.front: Who created UML and which body standardises it?
flashcards.back: The Three Amigos, Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson; it is standardised by the Object Management Group (OMG).
A visual representation of real-world conceptual classes, their associations and attributes, drawn as a UML class diagram without operations.

flashcards.front: When should you add a description class such as ProductDescription?
flashcards.back: When deleting the described instances would lose information, when many items share the same description, or to remove redundant data.

flashcards.front: Name the three strategies for identifying conceptual classes.
flashcards.back: Reuse or modify existing models, use a conceptual class category list, and noun phrase identification in use case text.

questions.questionText: Storing price, description and itemID in a separate class so that the price of a product is still known after every physical unit has been sold is an application of:
questions.explanation: A description class such as ProductDescription holds information about many instances, so it survives deletion of those instances and removes redundancy.

questions.questionText: Underlining the nouns and noun phrases in fully dressed use case text to find candidate conceptual classes is called:
questions.explanation: Noun phrase identification is Abbott's linguistic analysis technique; candidates must still be filtered because nouns may be synonyms or attributes.

questions.questionText: Which of the following should NOT appear in a Larman-style domain model?
options: Conceptual classes such as Sale and Payment
Associations such as Sale Paid-by Payment
Operations such as makeLineItem() on Sale
Attributes such as dateTime on Sale
questions.explanation: A domain model shows conceptual classes, associations and attributes only; responsibilities and methods belong to the design model.

questions.questionText: How many diagram types does UML 2.5 define?
questions.explanation: UML 2.5 has 14 diagram types: 7 structural (including profile, added in UML 2.2) and 7 behavioural; UML 1.x had 9 and UML 2.0 had 13.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a structural (static) UML diagram?
questions.explanation: The deployment diagram shows physical nodes and deployed artefacts, a static structure; the other three are interaction (behavioural) diagrams.

subtopics.title: Associations, Attributes & Representing System Behaviour
subtopics.subtitle: Associations, multiplicity, attributes, SSDs, operation contracts, state and activity diagrams

concepts.text: Adding Associations

An association is a relationship between classes (more precisely, between their instances) that indicates a meaningful and interesting connection. In a domain model, include associations for which knowledge of the relationship must be preserved for some duration (need-to-know associations) and those suggested by the common associations list, such as A is a transaction related to B, A is a line item of B, A is recorded in B, A is a member of B or A uses or manages B. Too many associations add visual noise, so avoid redundant or derivable ones.
Association notation and naming:
items: Drawn as a solid line between classes, named with a verb phrase in the ClassName-VerbPhrase-ClassName pattern, e.g. Sale Paid-by Payment, Register Records Sale.
An optional reading-direction arrow (small triangle) shows how to read the name; it says nothing about navigability.
Role names at each end describe the part an object plays, e.g. Person employee / employer Company.
Multiple associations between the same two classes are allowed, e.g. Flight Flies-to Airport and Flight Flies-from Airport.
A reflexive association links a class to itself, e.g. Employee manages Employee.

rows: A Team has 5..11 Players on the field list

concepts.latex: L_{min} = N \times lower,\quad L_{max} = N \times upper
concepts.plainText: L_min = N x lower bound, L_max = N x upper bound (links from N source objects)

rows: Weak whole-part (has-a); parts can exist independently and be shared
Strong whole-part; part belongs to one whole and is destroyed with it
is-a; subclass inherits from superclass (100% rule and is-a rule)
Solid line, hollow triangle at superclass
Dashed arrow to the used element

concepts.text: Adding Attributes

An attribute is a logical data value of an object, included when the requirements imply a need to remember the information, e.g. Sale needs dateTime. Attributes in a domain model should be simple data types such as Boolean, Date, Number, String, Time, or value-type data types such as Money, Address, Quantity or UPC. The key rule is: if we do not think of a concept as a number or text in the real world, it is probably a conceptual class, not an attribute; for example, a flight's destination is an Airport class, not a string. Derived attributes, computable from others, are prefixed with a slash, e.g. /total.

Do not use attributes to relate conceptual classes (e.g. a cashierID attribute on Register); show the relationship as an association. Foreign keys are a database design concern, not a domain modelling one.
System Sequence Diagrams and System Events

A system sequence diagram (SSD) shows, for one particular scenario of a use case, the events that external actors generate, their order and any inter-system events, treating the system as a black box. Each system event triggers a system operation, such as makeNewSale(), enterItem(itemID, quantity), endSale() and makePayment(amount) in Process Sale. SSDs are derived from use case text and give the system operations for which operation contracts are written and designs are created. Events should be named at the level of intent (enterItem) rather than the input mechanism (scan).

Cashier                     :System
   | makeNewSale()             |
   |-------------------------->|
   | loop [more items]         |
   | enterItem(itemID, qty)    |
   |-------------------------->|
   |<-- description, total ----|
   | endSale()                 |
   |-------------------------->|
   |<-- total with taxes ------|
   | makePayment(amount)       |
   |-------------------------->|
   |<-- change due, receipt ---|
Operation Contracts, State Machines and Activity Diagrams
An operation contract describes the effect of a system operation on domain objects, in sections:
items: Operation: name and parameters, e.g. enterItem(itemID: ItemID, quantity: integer); Cross references: related use cases.
Preconditions: noteworthy assumptions about the state of the system before the operation, e.g. there is an underway sale.

Postconditions: the state of domain objects after the operation, written declaratively in the past tense, in three categories: instance creation and deletion, attribute modification, and associations formed and broken.
Example: a SalesLineItem instance sli was created; sli was associated with the current Sale; sli.quantity became quantity; sli was associated with a ProductDescription based on itemID.

concepts.text: A UML state machine diagram shows the life cycle of one object or system: its states, the events that trigger transitions, guard conditions and actions, drawn as event [guard] / action on each transition, with a filled circle as the initial pseudo-state. It suits state-dependent objects such as a phone line, an order or a use case's legal sequence of system events. An activity diagram models workflows and business processes with actions, decisions and merges (diamonds), forks and joins (bars) for concurrency, and swimlanes (partitions) showing who performs each action.

formulas.latex: L_{min} = N \times lower,\quad L_{max} = N \times upper
formulas.plainText: L_min = N x lower bound, L_max = N x upper bound
Links in a many-to-many association between A and B <= |A| x |B|

notes.text: Operation contract postconditions describe changes to domain objects only: instances created or deleted, attributes modified, associations formed or broken. They never describe UI output or messages sent.
An SSD is drawn for one scenario, treats the system as a black box and shows only system events crossing the boundary; interactions between internal objects belong to design sequence diagrams.
Composition implies exclusive ownership and lifetime dependency (filled diamond); aggregation does not (hollow diamond). If a part can be shared or outlive the whole, it is not composition.

formulas.title: Link bounds from multiplicity
formulas.latex: L_{min} = N \times lower,\quad L_{max} = N \times upper
formulas.plainText: L_min = N x lower, L_max = N x upper
formulas.description: With N source objects and multiplicity lower..upper on the far end, the total links lie between N times each bound.

formulas.title: Many-to-many link limit
formulas.description: A * to * association between classes A and B can have at most one link per pair of instances.

formulas.title: Postcondition categories
formulas.plainText: Postconditions = instance creation/deletion + attribute modification + associations formed/broken
formulas.description: Every contract postcondition falls into one of these three categories of domain-object state change.

flashcards.front: What is a system sequence diagram?
flashcards.back: A diagram showing, for one use case scenario, the events external actors send to the system treated as a black box, in order.

flashcards.front: What are the three categories of operation contract postconditions?
flashcards.back: Instance creation or deletion, attribute modification, and associations formed or broken.

flashcards.front: How do you decide between an attribute and a conceptual class?
flashcards.back: If the concept is not thought of as a number or text in the real world, model it as a conceptual class with an association, not as an attribute.
Aggregation is a hollow diamond (parts independent); composition is a filled diamond (parts owned and destroyed with the whole).

questions.questionText: A system sequence diagram (SSD) in Larman's approach primarily shows:
options: System events sent by external actors to the system, treated as a black box, for one scenario
Messages exchanged between internal software objects to fulfil a system operation
The deployment of software artefacts onto hardware nodes
The life cycle states of a single domain object
questions.explanation: An SSD treats the system as a black box and shows the actor-generated system events for one use case scenario; internal object interactions appear in design sequence diagrams.

questions.questionText: Each Team is associated with Player with multiplicity 5..11 on the Player end. For 3 teams, the minimum and maximum number of Team–Player links are:
questions.explanation: Each of the 3 teams needs between 5 and 11 links, so the total lies between 3 × 5 = 15 and 3 × 11 = 33.

questions.questionText: In an airline domain model, how should the destination of a Flight be represented?
options: As a String attribute destination on Flight
As a foreign-key attribute destinationID on Flight
As an association Flight Flies-to Airport
As an operation getDestination() on Flight
questions.explanation: A destination airport is not thought of as a number or text in the real world, so it is a conceptual class Airport linked by an association; domain models avoid foreign keys and operations.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a valid postcondition in an operation contract for enterItem()?
options: A SalesLineItem instance sli was created
sli was associated with the current Sale
The item description and running total were displayed on the screen
questions.explanation: Postconditions describe state changes of domain objects (instances, attributes, associations); UI output is not a postcondition.
